title: The Gettysburg Address: central ideas, inference and word meaning
prompt: Read the excerpt, then choose the best answer for each question.

items.stem: Lincoln says, "It is altogether fitting and proper that we should do this." What does "fitting" mean here?

choices.text: the right size, like clothes
choices.misconception: uses the clothing meaning of "fitting", ignoring "and proper"

choices.text: right and suitable
exciting and fun
choices.misconception: ignores the solemn setting of honoring the dead

choices.text: about to happen soon
choices.misconception: guesses from "should do this" instead of the pairing with "proper"

items.stem: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the address?

choices.text: Lincoln's speech will be remembered forever
choices.misconception: reverses his point that the world will "little note" his words

choices.text: The cemetery must be finished quickly
choices.misconception: takes the occasion of the speech for its central idea

choices.text: Gettysburg was the most important battle of the war
choices.misconception: supplies a claim about the battle Lincoln never makes

choices.text: The living must honor the dead by finishing their work and keeping government by the people alive

items.stem: Lincoln says the soldiers consecrated the ground "far above our poor power to add or detract." What does this imply about the speakers' role at the ceremony?

choices.text: The speakers are too poor to pay for the cemetery
choices.misconception: takes "poor" as money, missing the comparison to the soldiers' deeds

choices.text: Their words can add nothing to what the soldiers' sacrifice already did
The speakers could take the ground's honor away
choices.misconception: misses "far above": nothing they say can detract

choices.text: Lincoln thinks the other speakers spoke badly
choices.misconception: infers criticism of other speakers that no line supports

items.stem: "The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here." What does "note" mean in this sentence?

choices.text: notice
a short written message
choices.misconception: uses the common noun meaning of "note", ignoring the sentence

choices.text: a musical sound
choices.misconception: picks the music meaning of "note", which doesn't fit "what we say"

choices.text: paper money
choices.misconception: takes "note" as a bank note, a meaning the sentence can't support

items.stem: Which two central ideas does Lincoln develop together in the address?

choices.text: Honoring the soldiers who died, and the living's duty to keep a nation built on liberty and equality
The history of the battle, and the plans for the train trip
choices.misconception: treats the occasion and the cover note's details as central ideas

choices.text: Lincoln's own career, and the cost of the war
choices.misconception: names ideas the address never develops

choices.text: The sadness of war, and the beauty of the battlefield
choices.misconception: picks a mood and a setting instead of developed ideas

items.stem: Lincoln says, "we can not consecrate... this ground." In this sentence, "consecrate" means

choices.text: capture in battle
choices.misconception: guesses from the battlefield setting instead of the pairing with "hallow"

choices.text: build on
choices.misconception: reads "consecrate" as "construct", ignoring "dedicate" and "hallow"

choices.text: describe in words
choices.misconception: guesses from the speeches being given, not the word's religious meaning

choices.text: make holy

items.stem: Lincoln says, "It is for us the living, rather, to be dedicated here to the unfinished work." What can you infer about his purpose?

choices.text: He wants the audience to finish building the cemetery
choices.misconception: takes "unfinished work" as construction

choices.text: He believes the war is already over
choices.misconception: contradicts "Now we are engaged in a great civil war"

choices.text: He turns a ceremony for the dead into a call to carry on the nation's cause
He blames the living for the soldiers' deaths
choices.misconception: infers blame that no line in the address supports

items.stem: The address moves from "Four score and seven years ago" to the present war to "a new birth of freedom." How does this order develop its central idea?

choices.text: It links past, present and future to show the living must carry the founders' ideals forward
It tells the battle's events in time order
choices.misconception: takes the time order for a battle account; no battle events appear

choices.text: It shows the founding is the main idea and the war a side detail
choices.misconception: weights one part instead of analyzing how the parts build together

choices.text: It shows Lincoln changing his mind during the speech
choices.misconception: reads the shift in time as a change of opinion

items.stem: What can you infer from Lincoln's note to Secretary Chase, printed before the address?

choices.text: Chase helped write the address
choices.misconception: infers co-authorship only because the note is addressed to him

choices.text: The trip to Gettysburg was still being arranged two days before the speech
Lincoln did not want to go to Gettysburg
choices.misconception: reads the not-yet-fixed start time as reluctance

choices.text: The address was given on November 17
choices.misconception: confuses the note's date with the address's November 19

items.stem: Which is the best objective summary of the address?

choices.text: In a moving and beautiful speech, Lincoln proves he is a great leader.
choices.misconception: adds praise and opinion, so the summary is not objective

choices.text: Lincoln tells Secretary Chase that a train will take them to Gettysburg.
choices.misconception: summarizes the cover note instead of the address

choices.text: Dedicating a battlefield cemetery, Lincoln says the soldiers made the ground sacred and the living must finish their work so government by the people survives.
Lincoln says the world will not remember his speech.
choices.misconception: gives one detail and leaves out the central ideas
